title: Function Transformer
abstract:
FunctionTransformer lets you use a custom feature transformation
inside a pipeline. This document covers the family of mathematical transforms
the notes list — log, reciprocal, square, square root and custom — explaining
for each what shape of data it fixes, why it works geometrically, the domain
restrictions that break it, and the Q-Q plot diagnostic that tells you whether it
worked. It also covers the inverse transform, which you must not forget when the
transform is applied to the target.

blocks.t: The Setting
From the notes

FunctionTransformer allows us to use custom feature
transformations inside the pipeline. "Function" here means a rule on the
data — e.g. $\log(x)$, $x/10000$.

Note: many ML algorithms work best and assume features are normally
distributed.
This topic covers the first column. Topic 19 covers the second.
Why normality matters at all
What "normal distribution" means here

The notes' picture: values cluster around the mean, with fewer values further
away. Symmetric, single peak, thin tails.

head: Algorithm
Why it prefers roughly-normal features
rows: The residuals are assumed normal for valid confidence intervals and $p$-values. Skewed inputs usually produce skewed residuals
Skew makes the loss surface poorly conditioned; convergence slows
A long tail dominates Euclidean distance, exactly as an unscaled feature does
The penalty treats all coefficients alike, which is only fair if features are comparably distributed

blocks.t: Trees do not care, and neither do many boosted models

Decision trees, random forests and gradient-boosted trees split on rank order.
Every transform here is monotone (on its valid domain), so the tree is
identical before and after. Applying a log transform for an XGBoost model
is not wrong; it is simply a no-op — with one exception: it changes nothing for
the features, but transforming the target does change what the model
optimises.
The Transforms

blocks.cap:
One right-skewed column under each transform. Log and square root pull
 the tail in; the reciprocal over-corrects into a new left skew; the square makes
 the problem worse.

blocks.t: Log transform
From the notes

The data becomes more normally distributed. Used on right-skewed data.
Not applicable on negative values.
Why it works

$\log$ is concave and monotone increasing. Its derivative $1/x$
decreases, so a fixed step in $x$ produces a smaller step in $\log x$ the larger
$x$ becomes. Concretely, an increase from $1$ to $10$ and from $1{,}000$ to
$10{,}000$ both become an increase of $\log 10$. Multiplicative structure in the
raw column becomes additive after the log:
\log(ab)=\log a+\log b .

This is exactly why it works on income, price, population and count data — all
of which are generated by multiplicative processes.

rows: Income, price, house area, city population, view counts, transaction amounts
Multiplicative outliers — an income of ₹$50$M becomes merely large rather than dominant

blocks.t: Reciprocal transform
From the notes

$\dfrac{1}{x}$ — the reciprocal compresses large values
aggressively.

It is stronger than the log, and it reverses order: the largest value
becomes the smallest. That reversal is occasionally exactly what you want —
converting a duration into a rate, for instance ($\text{speed} = \text{distance}/\text{time}$). Used blindly it usually over-corrects a right skew
into a left skew, as the figure above shows. Domain: $x\neq0$, and in practice
$x>0$.
Square transform
From the notes
$x^2$ — works best on left-skewed data.

$x^2$ is convex: it stretches large values apart and compresses small ones
— the opposite of the log. That is precisely what a left-skewed column needs.

blocks.cap:
Left-skewed data requires the opposite treatment. Squaring corrects it;
 applying a log — the reflex for skew — makes it substantially worse.

blocks.t: Match the transform to the direction of the skew

The single most common mistake with this family is reaching for the log whenever
a distribution "looks wrong". Check the sign of the skewness first:
positive skew (long right tail) $\Rightarrow$ concave transform (log,
sqrt, reciprocal). Negative skew (long left tail) $\Rightarrow$ convex
transform (square, cube), or reflect the column first and then apply a log.
Square root transform
From the notes

$\sqrt{x}$ — for count or mildly skewed data, especially when zeros are
present.

Milder than the log, and it is defined at $x=0$ — which is why it is the
default choice for count columns, where zeros are common and a log would be
undefined.
The variance-stabilising justification

For Poisson-distributed counts, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}[X]=\lambda$ —
the variance grows with the mean, which violates the constant-variance assumption
of linear models. The delta method gives, for a transform $g$,
\operatorname{Var} \left(g(X)\right)\approx \left(g'(\lambda)\right)^2\lambda .
Setting $g=\sqrt{\cdot}$ gives $g'(\lambda)=\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt\lambda}$, so
\operatorname{Var}(\sqrt X)\approx\frac{\lambda}{4\lambda}=\frac14,

a constant independent of $\lambda$. The square root is the
variance-stabilising transform for count data, not merely a convenient
one. By the same argument, the log is variance-stabilising when the standard
deviation is proportional to the mean.
Custom
From the notes
Any custom logic.

This is the general case, and in practice the most valuable one: clipping,
ratios, differences of dates, binning by a domain rule, a signed log
$\operatorname{sign}(x)\log(1+|x|)$ that handles negatives. Anything you can
write as a function of the column.
Choosing and Verifying

blocks.cap:
The transforms plotted as functions. The curvature is the whole story:
 concave functions compress the right tail; convex functions expand it.

blocks.t: The Q-Q plot

blocks.cap:
A Q-Q plot compares your data's quantiles against a normal
 distribution's. Points on the diagonal mean normal. An upward-curving tail on
 the right means right skew. This is a far better diagnostic than a histogram,
 because deviations in the tails are visible rather than compressed.

blocks.t:
Complement it with a numeric test — scipy.stats.skew before and after,
and the Shapiro–Wilk or D'Agostino test for normality — but always look at the
plot. On large samples every normality test rejects, because no real data is
exactly normal; what matters is whether it is close enough.
Transforming the Target
If you log the target, you must invert it — and correct the bias

Log-transforming a right-skewed target (house price, salary, claim amount) is
common and effective. Two things follow.

1. You must invert before reporting. An RMSE in log-units is
meaningless to a stakeholder. Use TransformedTargetRegressor, which
applies func before fitting and inverse_func after predicting,
automatically.

2. $\exp$ of the mean is not the mean. By Jensen's inequality,
$\mathbb{E}[e^{Z}] > e^{\mathbb{E}[Z]}$. Naively exponentiating the predicted log
gives the median, not the mean, and systematically under-predicts. If
residuals are approximately normal with variance $\sigma^2$, the
smearing-corrected estimate is
\hat y = \exp \left(\hat z + \tfrac{\sigma^2}{2}\right).

Whether you want the median or the mean is a business decision — but you should
know which one you are reporting.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer, StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer, TransformedTargetRegressor
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = rng.lognormal(3.2, .85, 5000)              # right-skewed, like income

# =====================================================================
# 1. DIAGNOSE FIRST -- what direction is the skew?
# =====================================================================
def diagnose(v, name=""):
    v = np.asarray(v, dtype=float)
    sk = stats.skew(v)
    direction = ("RIGHT (positive)" if sk > .5 else
                 "LEFT (negative)"  if sk < -.5 else "roughly symmetric")
    print(f"{name:22s} skew {sk:+6.2f}  {direction}")
    return sk

diagnose(x, "original")
for name, f in [("log", np.log), ("sqrt", np.sqrt),
                ("reciprocal", lambda v: 1/v), ("square", np.square)]:
    diagnose(f(x), name)
# original   +5.28  RIGHT   -> needs a CONCAVE transform
# log        +0.01  symmetric        <- the winner
# sqrt       +1.44  still right
# reciprocal -1.02  OVER-corrected into left skew
# square    +21.3   much worse

# =====================================================================
# 2. FunctionTransformer -- the pipeline-compatible wrapper
# =====================================================================
log_tf = FunctionTransformer(func=np.log1p,        # log(1+x): safe at zero
                             inverse_func=np.expm1, # the exact inverse
                             validate=True,
                             feature_names_out="one-to-one")
X = x.reshape(-1, 1)
Xt = log_tf.fit_transform(X)
print("round-trips exactly:", np.allclose(log_tf.inverse_transform(Xt), X))

# All five from the notes, as reusable objects:
transformers = {
    "log":        FunctionTransformer(np.log1p,  inverse_func=np.expm1),
    "reciprocal": FunctionTransformer(lambda v: 1/(v+1e-9)),
    "square":     FunctionTransformer(np.square, inverse_func=np.sqrt),
    "sqrt":       FunctionTransformer(np.sqrt,   inverse_func=np.square),
    "custom":     FunctionTransformer(lambda v: np.sign(v)*np.log1p(np.abs(v))),
}
# The "custom" one is a SIGNED log -- it handles negative values, which
# plain log cannot. This is the pattern for real custom logic.

# =====================================================================
# 3. THE DOMAIN RESTRICTIONS THAT BITE
# =====================================================================
with_zero = np.array([0., 1., 5., 100.])
print("log(0)  =", np.log(with_zero[:1]))         # -inf  -> breaks the model
print("log1p(0)=", np.log1p(with_zero[:1]))       # 0.0   -> correct

negatives = np.array([-5., 0., 5.])
print("log of negatives:", np.log(negatives))     # nan
print("signed log      :",
      np.sign(negatives) * np.log1p(np.abs(negatives)))   # works

# GUARD: fail loudly at fit time rather than producing NaN silently
def safe_log(v):
    v = np.asarray(v, dtype=float)
    if (v <= -1).any():
        raise ValueError("log1p requires x > -1; clip or use the signed log")
    return np.log1p(v)

# =====================================================================
# 4. DOES IT ACTUALLY IMPROVE THE MODEL?
# =====================================================================
n = 4000
income = rng.lognormal(10.5, .9, n)
age    = rng.uniform(20, 65, n)
y = (0.35 * np.log(income) + 0.04 * age + rng.normal(0, .8, n) > 4.5).astype(int)
Xr = np.c_[income, age]

raw = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
logged = Pipeline([
    ("log",   ColumnTransformer([("l", FunctionTransformer(np.log1p), [0])],
                                remainder="passthrough")),
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("clf",   LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)),
])
print("raw    cv auc:", cross_val_score(raw,    Xr, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4))
print("logged cv auc:", cross_val_score(logged, Xr, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4))

# The same comparison for a TREE -- expect no difference at all:
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
rf_raw = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=100, random_state=0)
print("tree raw   :", cross_val_score(rf_raw, Xr, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4))
print("tree logged:", cross_val_score(rf_raw, np.c_[np.log1p(income), age], y,
                                      cv=5, scoring="roc_auc").mean().round(4))
# Nearly identical -- a monotone transform cannot change rank-based splits.

# =====================================================================
# 5. TRANSFORMING THE TARGET -- and inverting it automatically
# =====================================================================
price = np.exp(0.9 * np.log(income) + rng.normal(0, .35, n))   # skewed target
Xp = np.c_[np.log1p(income), age]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xp, price, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

plain = LinearRegression().fit(Xtr, ytr)
ttr = TransformedTargetRegressor(regressor=LinearRegression(),
                                 func=np.log1p, inverse_func=np.expm1).fit(Xtr, ytr)

from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error
print("plain     MAE:", round(mean_absolute_error(yte, plain.predict(Xte)), 1))
print("log-target MAE:", round(mean_absolute_error(yte, ttr.predict(Xte)), 1))
# Predictions come back in RUPEES, not log-rupees. The inversion is automatic.

# THE JENSEN CORRECTION -- exp(mean) is the median, not the mean
z = np.log1p(ytr)
resid_var = np.var(z - np.log1p(ttr.predict(Xtr)))
naive     = np.expm1(np.log1p(ttr.predict(Xte)))
smeared   = np.expm1(np.log1p(ttr.predict(Xte)) + resid_var / 2)
print("naive back-transform predicts the MEDIAN, mean of preds:", naive.mean().round(1))
print("smearing-corrected (targets the MEAN)      :", smeared.mean().round(1))
print("actual mean                                :", yte.mean().round(1))

# =====================================================================
# 6. VERIFY WITH A Q-Q PLOT AND A TEST
# =====================================================================
for name, v in [("original", x), ("log", np.log(x)), ("sqrt", np.sqrt(x))]:
    stat, p = stats.normaltest(v)
    print(f"{name:9s} skew {stats.skew(v):+6.2f}  "
          f"D'Agostino p={p:.2e}  {'NOT normal' if p < .05 else 'plausibly normal'}")
# On n=5000 almost everything rejects. Judge by the Q-Q plot and the skew,
# not by the p-value alone.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
FunctionTransformer allows custom feature transformations
 inside the pipeline. "Function" means a rule on the data.

Many ML algorithms work best and assume features are normally
 distributed — gradient-based, distance-based and Gaussian models.
 Trees are indifferent.

Log: makes data more normal, for right-skewed data,
 not applicable to negatives. Use log1p when zeros exist.

Reciprocal $1/x$: compresses large values aggressively,
 and reverses order.
Square $x^2$: works best on left-skewed data.

Square root $\sqrt{x}$: for count or mildly skewed data,
 especially when zeros are present. It is the variance-stabilising
 transform for Poisson counts.
Custom: any logic — clipping, ratios, signed log.

Match the transform to the direction of the skew: concave for
 right skew, convex for left skew.
Verify with a Q-Q plot and the skewness value, before and after.

If you transform the target, invert it before reporting, and
 remember that $\exp$ of the mean prediction is the median.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Your income column is heavily right-skewed. What do you do?

Apply a log transform — log1p if there are zeros. Income is generated
multiplicatively, so a log turns that structure additive and produces a roughly
normal column. Verify with a Q-Q plot and the skewness before and after.
Q. Log-transforming your features did nothing for XGBoost. Why?

Trees split on rank order, and the log is monotone, so every split threshold maps
across and the tree is identical. Transforms of this family help gradient-based
and distance-based models, not tree-based ones.
Q. The column contains zeros and you need a log. What now?

np.log1p(x) $=\log(1+x)$, which is defined at zero and maps $0\mapsto0$.
Adding an arbitrary constant such as $\log(x+1000)$ also works but the constant
is a hidden hyperparameter that changes the shape.
Q. When would you use the square transform?

On left-skewed data — a long tail towards low values. Examination scores near a
ceiling and age at death are typical. Applying a log there makes it worse.

Q. You log-transformed the target and predictions are systematically too
low. Why?

Jensen's inequality: exponentiating the predicted mean of the logs gives the
median of the original distribution, not the mean. Apply a smearing correction,
$\exp(\hat z + \sigma^2/2)$, if the business wants the mean.
Q. Should you transform features before or after scaling?

Before. Reshape the distribution first, then standardise it. Scaling is the last
step of the feature-engineering pipeline (Topic 12).
